The measure's seven criteria for the institute describe the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy at UCLA:
Prop 38 does not name the institute that would receive half its money. Instead, section 130353 of the text lists seven criteria the Department of Public Health must apply. The institute must:
Be a 501(c)(3) medical research institute "in existence as of January 1, 2025" that was "founded for the primary purpose of, and specializes specifically in" immunology and immunotherapy research.
Have an affiliation agreement, signed "not later than January 1, 2025," with a University of California campus that has a graduate program in immunology, a public health care system that runs its own clinical trials, and "a hospital and clinic volume of greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year."
Be governed by a board whose bylaws, adopted by January 1, 2025, include "multiple members who are senior-level representatives" of that campus or its health system.
Own or lease, as of January 1, 2026, a site of at least 200,000 square feet intended as its research facility.
Agree to conduct collaborative research with other California nonprofit centers, including multi-institutional clinical trials.
Have identified, in the affiliation agreement, at least $250 million in philanthropic donations or fundraising commitments.
Have secured at least $50 million for "a rapid vaccine development program" and at least $50 million for "a microbiome research program."
The LAO's December letter counted "at least ten research centers in California" working in the field, "at least three" of which specialize in it. The public record on one of them lines up with the list.
On August 28, 2024, UCLA announced (https://externalaffairs.ucla.edu/?p=3572) a $120 million commitment from Dr. Gary Michelson, a retired spinal surgeon and inventor, and his wife Alya to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, a 501(c)(3) "governed by an independent board that includes UCLA representatives." The release described $50 million for a rapid vaccine development entity and $50 million for a microbiome entity within the institute, plus a $20 million endowment for young scientists, and said the institute would occupy 360,000 square feet of the 700,000-square-foot UCLA Research Park on the site of the former Westside Pavilion mall, which UCLA acquired in January 2024 with the help of a $200 million state appropriation. Michelson is the institute's co-founder and board chair; the release lists Meyer Luskin, Dr. Eric Esrailian, Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Michael Milken and Sean Parker as co-founders.
UCLA Health's September 2026 fact sheet (https://www.uclahealth.org/sites/default/files/documents/07/2026-09-30-1734700-ucla-health-fact-sheet-2026-final-digital.pdf) reports more than 46,000 inpatient admissions and more than 4.4 million outpatient clinic visits a year across five hospitals. CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california) in July that UCSF's medical center had 3.4 million outpatient visits, below the measure's 3.5 million line, and that UCLA spokesperson Phil Hampton confirmed the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is the only UCLA-affiliated nonprofit that could meet the criteria. Yes on 38 spokesperson Claudia Briggs told the outlet: "We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding," and "We can't speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California."
The institute's own tax filings (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093), which the IRS makes public, fill in the rest. The IRS recognized it as tax-exempt in August 2022. Its Form 990 for the year ending June 30, 2025, filed May 1, 2026, discloses that it "signed an affiliation agreement with the Regents of the University of California … by and on behalf of UCLA and UCLA Health," under which its board consists of six "Founders Directors" and four "UCLA Directors" appointed by the university, with the UCLA directors holding veto rights over actions that could harm the university. The ten unpaid directors include Michelson as chair, Esrailian as president, Luskin as treasurer, UCLA Health chief executive John Mazziotta and UCLA Chancellor Julio Frenk.
The same filings show how small the institute's own operation still is. It reported revenue of $1.1 million in the year ending June 2023, $1.0 million in the year ending June 2024, and $20 million, all contributions, in the year ending June 2025, against expenses of $1.6 million that year. It ended June 2025 with net assets of $19.1 million and reported no employees. Michelson's $120 million commitment does not appear on those books because, as UCLA's release states, "The David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA receives the gift." CalMatters reported that the institute told it it had $250 million in philanthropic support, the amount criterion six requires.
Gary Michelson is also the measure's official proponent, listed by the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) on A.G. File 25-0026, and the principal funder of both its petition drive and its campaign.
The institute would not be a public agency under California's open-records and open-meeting laws:
Section 130363 of the text states that "the institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law," and names three laws by their code sections: the California Public Records Act, the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act and the Political Reform Act. The grant council, by contrast, is covered by the Political Reform Act, with two carve-outs: a member may vote on grants to entities in the same field as their employer, and may vote on research into a disease they or a family member has. Government Code section 1090, the conflict-of-interest law for public contracts, applies to the council only when a grant directly benefits a member and the member fails to recuse.
The measure attaches its own accountability rules in place of those laws. The institute must publish an annual report on its website and commission an independent audit each year, which the Controller reviews at a public meeting. The council must do the same, with audits of a random 10% of grantees. A six-member Citizens' Financial Accountability Oversight Committee, chaired by the Controller with appointees of the State Auditor, Treasurer, Senate leader, Assembly Speaker and council chair, reviews the audits and issues its own annual report. The No campaign, co-chaired (https://votenoonprop38.org/) by former National Institutes of Health associate director Robert Kaplan and health-policy consultant David Panush, makes the public-agency exemption one of its four main arguments.
Proposition 38's repayment promise rests on a 10% royalty to the state and a 20% California discount:
The Yes campaign's claim that the bond is "designed to pay for itself" comes from section 130358. Any recipient of research funds must pay the state 10% of "all revenues" from selling or licensing intellectual property that arises from funded research, within 30 days of receiving the money, "without regard to whether the research … was funded wholly or only in part" by the measure. Those payments go into the General Fund until they equal the bonds' principal plus interest, then into the research fund for future grants. Licensing deals must return royalties of at least 10% of gross revenues to the recipient (the Department of Public Health can approve as low as 5%), and joint ventures must return at least 25% of gross profits. The selected institute, "in consultation with the department," runs a licensing program to "maximize the revenue" and serves as "a clearinghouse and approval center" for every commercialization agreement under the measure.
The discount works in two stages. For the first 12 months of commercial sales, California patients, hospitals and insurers may not be charged more than the price anywhere else in the United States. After that, the first nine months of sales data set a "national average price, excluding California," and the California price must sit at least 20% below it, recalculated every year.
The LAO does not treat the royalty as a repayment plan. Revenue "is uncertain but could be significant," its analysis says, and "the timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state's bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades." Its ballot summary says the state "could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades." The reference point in California's own history is CIRM's first royalty check, $190,345.87, 14 years after Prop 71.
LAO fiscal estimate changed from $500 million a year for 25 years to $500 million to $600 million for about 20 years:
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) estimates the General Fund cost of repaying the bond at "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years," about one-quarter of 1% of the state's General Fund budget, with the total cost "about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation)" than paying up front. Its December 17, 2025 letter to the Attorney General, written when the measure was still a petition, said "about $500 million each year over a 25-year period." That earlier figure is the one printed on the petition and in the ballot argument against the measure, which says taxpayers "would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years." The two are different versions of the same estimate, not a disagreement.
The LAO also flags indirect effects it cannot size: new treatments could raise or lower costs for Medi-Cal, and the in-state purchasing rule could lift employment and taxable income. The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) puts the measure in context: the state is repaying about $80 billion of General Fund bonds, has about $40 billion more authorized but unsold, and pays about $6 billion a year in debt service, about 3% of General Fund revenue. Propositions 1 and 38 together would add about $1 billion a year, about half of 1%.
Proposition 38's Yes side reports $76.2 million from its top donors and its only opposition committee $3,782:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $76.2 million in support of Prop 38 from two committees, the largest support figure for any measure on the ballot except Proposition 42. The main committee, "Yes on 38: Californians for Life-Saving Immunology Research and Cures, sponsored by the Michelson Center for Public Policy," lists four top contributors: Gary K. Michelson, $40 million; the Michelson Center for Public Policy's own Yes on 38 committee, $21.2 million, whose top contributor is Michelson; Meyer Luskin, $5 million; and the California Democratic Party, $15,595.20. The Center's committee lists one contributor, Michelson, at $10 million. Luskin is the institute's co-founder and treasurer.
The FPPC lists no opposing committee because none has reached the $1 million reporting threshold. The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-38-authorizes-bonds-immunology-research-initiative-statut), which counts all reported contributions through October 6, shows $64.2 million for the two Yes committees and $3,782 for the committee "No on Proposition 38." The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "Californians for Immunology Research and Cures, sponsored by the Michelson Center for Public Policy," with major funding from Michelson, his affiliated entity and Luskin, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2006-top-funders-02-25-26.pdf) filing.
The arguments over Proposition 38 pit federal research cuts against ballot-box science:
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Susan Disney Lord of Alzheimer's Los Angeles, Eugene P. Brandon of the ALS Association and Dr. Brian Shuch of the Kidney Cancer Association, says "massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research" and that Prop 38 "creates a stable source of funding." It says the measure "is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS," cites the 20% discount, the 2% administrative cap, the audits and the bar on for-profit grantees, and promises "tens of thousands of good-paying jobs." Quoted supporters include Stanford immunologist Mark Davis and cancer survivor Laurie Adami. The rebuttal to the No argument repeats that "YES ON 38 IS DESIGNED TO PAY FOR ITSELF."
The No argument, signed by Robert M. California is the exception among states. Voters approved Proposition 71 in 2004, which authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem cell research and created the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, and Proposition 14 in 2020, which added $5.5 billion. Both were citizen initiatives. CIRM describes itself as a "taxpayer-funded agency" with a public governing board, and its revenue-sharing rules sent the state its first royalty check (https://blog.cirm.ca.gov/2018/02/12/california-gets-first-royalty-check-from-stem-cell-agency-investments/), for $190,345.87, in February 2018, 14 years after Prop 71 passed.
A third research bond is already on the calendar. Senate Bill 895, by Senator Scott Wiener, passed both houses on August 31 and was signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/30/at-the-top-of-the-golden-gate-bridge-governor-newsom-signs-his-final-bill-investing-in-californias-next-generation-of-innovation/) by Governor Newsom on September 30 as the last bill of the session. It places a $7.5 billion science and health research bond on the March 7, 2028 primary ballot and creates a California Foundation for Science and Health Research inside the Government Operations Agency to award grants, loans and contracts across "biomedical, behavioral health, and climate research" and other fields, with the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act applying to its council, according to the chaptered bill (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/sb895-ch1040.pdf). The measure's seven criteria for the institute describe the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy at UCLA:
Prop 38 does not name the institute that would receive half its money. Instead, section 130353 of the text lists seven criteria the Department of Public Health must apply. The institute must:
Be a 501(c)(3) medical research institute "in existence as of January 1, 2025" that was "founded for the primary purpose of, and specializes specifically in" immunology and immunotherapy research.
Have an affiliation agreement, signed "not later than January 1, 2025," with a University of California campus that has a graduate program in immunology, a public health care system that runs its own clinical trials, and "a hospital and clinic volume of greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year."
Be governed by a board whose bylaws, adopted by January 1, 2025, include "multiple members who are senior-level representatives" of that campus or its health system.
Own or lease, as of January 1, 2026, a site of at least 200,000 square feet intended as its research facility.
Agree to conduct collaborative research with other California nonprofit centers, including multi-institutional clinical trials.
Have identified, in the affiliation agreement, at least $250 million in philanthropic donations or fundraising commitments.
Have secured at least $50 million for "a rapid vaccine development program" and at least $50 million for "a microbiome research program."
The LAO's December letter counted "at least ten research centers in California" working in the field, "at least three" of which specialize in it. The public record on one of them lines up with the list.
On August 28, 2024, UCLA announced (https://externalaffairs.ucla.edu/?p=3572) a $120 million commitment from Dr. Gary Michelson, a retired spinal surgeon and inventor, and his wife Alya to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, a 501(c)(3) "governed by an independent board that includes UCLA representatives." The release described $50 million for a rapid vaccine development entity and $50 million for a microbiome entity within the institute, plus a $20 million endowment for young scientists, and said the institute would occupy 360,000 square feet of the 700,000-square-foot UCLA Research Park on the site of the former Westside Pavilion mall, which UCLA acquired in January 2024 with the help of a $200 million state appropriation. Michelson is the institute's co-founder and board chair; the release lists Meyer Luskin, Dr. Eric Esrailian, Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Michael Milken and Sean Parker as co-founders.
UCLA Health's September 2026 fact sheet (https://www.uclahealth.org/sites/default/files/documents/07/2026-09-30-1734700-ucla-health-fact-sheet-2026-final-digital.pdf) reports more than 46,000 inpatient admissions and more than 4.4 million outpatient clinic visits a year across five hospitals. CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california) in July that UCSF's medical center had 3.4 million outpatient visits, below the measure's 3.5 million line, and that UCLA spokesperson Phil Hampton confirmed the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is the only UCLA-affiliated nonprofit that could meet the criteria. Yes on 38 spokesperson Claudia Briggs told the outlet: "We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding," and "We can't speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California."
The institute's own tax filings (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093), which the IRS makes public, fill in the rest. The IRS recognized it as tax-exempt in August 2022. Its Form 990 for the year ending June 30, 2025, filed May 1, 2026, discloses that it "signed an affiliation agreement with the Regents of the University of California … by and on behalf of UCLA and UCLA Health," under which its board consists of six "Founders Directors" and four "UCLA Directors" appointed by the university, with the UCLA directors holding veto rights over actions that could harm the university. The ten unpaid directors include Michelson as chair, Esrailian as president, Luskin as treasurer, UCLA Health chief executive John Mazziotta and UCLA Chancellor Julio Frenk.
The same filings show how small the institute's own operation still is. It reported revenue of $1.1 million in the year ending June 2023, $1.0 million in the year ending June 2024, and $20 million, all contributions, in the year ending June 2025, against expenses of $1.6 million that year. It ended June 2025 with net assets of $19.1 million and reported no employees. Michelson's $120 million commitment does not appear on those books because, as UCLA's release states, "The David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA receives the gift." CalMatters reported that the institute told it it had $250 million in philanthropic support, the amount criterion six requires.
Gary Michelson is also the measure's official proponent, listed by the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) on A.G. File 25-0026, and the principal funder of both its petition drive and its campaign.
The institute would not be a public agency under California's open-records and open-meeting laws:
Section 130363 of the text states that "the institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law," and names three laws by their code sections: the California Public Records Act, the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act and the Political Reform Act. The grant council, by contrast, is covered by the Political Reform Act, with two carve-outs: a member may vote on grants to entities in the same field as their employer, and may vote on research into a disease they or a family member has. Government Code section 1090, the conflict-of-interest law for public contracts, applies to the council only when a grant directly benefits a member and the member fails to recuse.
The measure attaches its own accountability rules in place of those laws. The institute must publish an annual report on its website and commission an independent audit each year, which the Controller reviews at a public meeting. The council must do the same, with audits of a random 10% of grantees. A six-member Citizens' Financial Accountability Oversight Committee, chaired by the Controller with appointees of the State Auditor, Treasurer, Senate leader, Assembly Speaker and council chair, reviews the audits and issues its own annual report. The No campaign, co-chaired (https://votenoonprop38.org/) by former National Institutes of Health associate director Robert Kaplan and health-policy consultant David Panush, makes the public-agency exemption one of its four main arguments.
Proposition 38's repayment promise rests on a 10% royalty to the state and a 20% California discount:
The Yes campaign's claim that the bond is "designed to pay for itself" comes from section 130358. Any recipient of research funds must pay the state 10% of "all revenues" from selling or licensing intellectual property that arises from funded research, within 30 days of receiving the money, "without regard to whether the research … was funded wholly or only in part" by the measure. Those payments go into the General Fund until they equal the bonds' principal plus interest, then into the research fund for future grants. Licensing deals must return royalties of at least 10% of gross revenues to the recipient (the Department of Public Health can approve as low as 5%), and joint ventures must return at least 25% of gross profits. The selected institute, "in consultation with the department," runs a licensing program to "maximize the revenue" and serves as "a clearinghouse and approval center" for every commercialization agreement under the measure.
The discount works in two stages. For the first 12 months of commercial sales, California patients, hospitals and insurers may not be charged more than the price anywhere else in the United States. After that, the first nine months of sales data set a "national average price, excluding California," and the California price must sit at least 20% below it, recalculated every year.
The LAO does not treat the royalty as a repayment plan. Revenue "is uncertain but could be significant," its analysis says, and "the timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state's bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades." Its ballot summary says the state "could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades." The reference point in California's own history is CIRM's first royalty check, $190,345.87, 14 years after Prop 71.
LAO fiscal estimate changed from $500 million a year for 25 years to $500 million to $600 million for about 20 years:

In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.

Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for

In summary

The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.

California is the exception among states. Voters approved Proposition 71 in 2004, which authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem cell research and created the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, and Proposition 14 in 2020, which added $5.5 billion. Both were citizen initiatives. CIRM describes itself as a "taxpayer-funded agency" with a public governing board, and its revenue-sharing rules sent the state its first royalty check (https://blog.cirm.ca.gov/2018/02/12/california-gets-first-royalty-check-from-stem-cell-agency-investments/), for $190,345.87, in February 2018, 14 years after Prop 71 passed.
A third research bond is already on the calendar. Senate Bill 895, by Senator Scott Wiener, passed both houses on August 31 and was signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/30/at-the-top-of-the-golden-gate-bridge-governor-newsom-signs-his-final-bill-investing-in-californias-next-generation-of-innovation/) by Governor Newsom on September 30 as the last bill of the session. It places a $7.5 billion science and health research bond on the March 7, 2028 primary ballot and creates a California Foundation for Science and Health Research inside the Government Operations Agency to award grants, loans and contracts across "biomedical, behavioral health, and climate research" and other fields, with the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act applying to its council, according to the chaptered bill (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/sb895-ch1040.pdf). If Prop 38 passes, voters will have been asked to approve $15.9 billion of research bonds in 16 months.
California's research bonds compared, from Proposition 71 to the 2028 SB 895 bond:
Feature Propositions 71 (2004) and 14 (2020) Proposition 38 (November 2026) SB 895 bond (March 2028 ballot)
Amount borrowed $3 billion, then $5.5 billion ($8.5 billion combined) $8.4 billion $7.5 billion
Field Stem cell research Immunology and immunotherapy; at least $4.2 billion on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's Biomedical, behavioral health, climate and other research fields
How it reached voters Citizen initiatives Citizen initiative (petition paid for by a Michelson-sponsored committee) Legislature; signed September 30, 2026
Who awards the money CIRM, a state agency with a public governing board Half to one nonprofit institute chosen by the Department of Public Health; half as competitive grants chosen by a council of 17 to 22 university representatives A new state foundation in the Government Operations Agency, through grants, loans and contracts
Open-records and open-meeting laws Apply (state agency) The institute "shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law"; the council is covered by the Political Reform Act Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act applies to the council and peer-review panels
Money back to the state Revenue sharing; first royalty check of $190,345.87 arrived in 2018, 14 years after Prop 71 10% of revenue from funded discoveries goes to the General Fund until the bond plus interest is repaid Council sets intellectual-property standards so the state can "benefit" from inventions and royalties
Legislative Analyst's cost Not applicable $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years Not yet analyzed for the ballot
The measure's seven criteria for the institute describe the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy at UCLA:
Prop 38 does not name the institute that would receive half its money. Instead, section 130353 of the text lists seven criteria the Department of Public Health must apply. The institute must:
Be a 501(c)(3) medical research institute "in existence as of January 1, 2025" that was "founded for the primary purpose of, and specializes specifically in" immunology and immunotherapy research.
Have an affiliation agreement, signed "not later than January 1, 2025," with a University of California campus that has a graduate program in immunology, a public health care system that runs its own clinical trials, and "a hospital and clinic volume of greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year."
Be governed by a board whose bylaws, adopted by January 1, 2025, include "multiple members who are senior-level representatives" of that campus or its health system.
Own or lease, as of January 1, 2026, a site of at least 200,000 square feet intended as its research facility.
Agree to conduct collaborative research with other California nonprofit centers, including multi-institutional clinical trials.
Have identified, in the affiliation agreement, at least $250 million in philanthropic donations or fundraising commitments.
Have secured at least $50 million for "a rapid vaccine development program" and at least $50 million for "a microbiome research program."
The LAO's December letter counted "at least ten research centers in California" working in the field, "at least three" of which specialize in it. The public record on one of them lines up with the list.
On August 28, 2024, UCLA announced (https://externalaffairs.ucla.edu/?p=3572) a $120 million commitment from Dr. Gary Michelson, a retired spinal surgeon and inventor, and his wife Alya to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, a 501(c)(3) "governed by an independent board that includes UCLA representatives." The release described $50 million for a rapid vaccine development entity and $50 million for a microbiome entity within the institute, plus a $20 million endowment for young scientists, and said the institute would occupy 360,000 square feet of the 700,000-square-foot UCLA Research Park on the site of the former Westside Pavilion mall, which UCLA acquired in January 2024 with the help of a $200 million state appropriation. Michelson is the institute's co-founder and board chair; the release lists Meyer Luskin, Dr. Eric Esrailian, Dr. Arie Belldegrun, Michael Milken and Sean Parker as co-founders.
UCLA Health's September 2026 fact sheet (https://www.uclahealth.org/sites/default/files/documents/07/2026-09-30-1734700-ucla-health-fact-sheet-2026-final-digital.pdf) reports more than 46,000 inpatient admissions and more than 4.4 million outpatient clinic visits a year across five hospitals. CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california) in July that UCSF's medical center had 3.4 million outpatient visits, below the measure's 3.5 million line, and that UCLA spokesperson Phil Hampton confirmed the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is the only UCLA-affiliated nonprofit that could meet the criteria. Yes on 38 spokesperson Claudia Briggs told the outlet: "We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding," and "We can't speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California."
The institute's own tax filings (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093), which the IRS makes public, fill in the rest. The IRS recognized it as tax-exempt in August 2022. Its Form 990 for the year ending June 30, 2025, filed May 1, 2026, discloses that it "signed an affiliation agreement with the Regents of the University of California … by and on behalf of UCLA and UCLA Health," under which its board consists of six "Founders Directors" and four "UCLA Directors" appointed by the university, with the UCLA directors holding veto rights over actions that could harm the university. The ten unpaid directors include Michelson as chair, Esrailian as president, Luskin as treasurer, UCLA Health chief executive John Mazziotta and UCLA Chancellor Julio Frenk.
The same filings show how small the institute's own operation still is. It reported revenue of $1.1 million in the year ending June 2023, $1.0 million in the year ending June 2024, and $20 million, all contributions, in the year ending June 2025, against expenses of $1.6 million that year. It ended June 2025 with net assets of $19.1 million and reported no employees. Michelson's $120 million commitment does not appear on those books because, as UCLA's release states, "The David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA receives the gift." CalMatters reported that the institute told it it had $250 million in philanthropic support, the amount criterion six requires.
Gary Michelson is also the measure's official proponent, listed by the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/initiatives/active-measures) on A.G. File 25-0026, and the principal funder of both its petition drive and its campaign.
The institute would not be a public agency under California's open-records and open-meeting laws:
Section 130363 of the text states that "the institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law," and names three laws by their code sections: the California Public Records Act, the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act and the Political Reform Act. The grant council, by contrast, is covered by the Political Reform Act, with two carve-outs: a member may vote on grants to entities in the same field as their employer, and may vote on research into a disease they or a family member has. Government Code section 1090, the conflict-of-interest law for public contracts, applies to the council only when a grant directly benefits a member and the member fails to recuse.
The measure attaches its own accountability rules in place of those laws. The institute must publish an annual report on its website and commission an independent audit each year, which the Controller reviews at a public meeting. The council must do the same, with audits of a random 10% of grantees. A six-member Citizens' Financial Accountability Oversight Committee, chaired by the Controller with appointees of the State Auditor, Treasurer, Senate leader, Assembly Speaker and council chair, reviews the audits and issues its own annual report. The No campaign, co-chaired (https://votenoonprop38.org/) by former National Institutes of Health associate director Robert Kaplan and health-policy consultant David Panush, makes the public-agency exemption one of its four main arguments.
Proposition 38's repayment promise rests on a 10% royalty to the state and a 20% California discount:
The Yes campaign's claim that the bond is "designed to pay for itself" comes from section 130358. Any recipient of research funds must pay the state 10% of "all revenues" from selling or licensing intellectual property that arises from funded research, within 30 days of receiving the money, "without regard to whether the research … was funded wholly or only in part" by the measure. Those payments go into the General Fund until they equal the bonds' principal plus interest, then into the research fund for future grants. Licensing deals must return royalties of at least 10% of gross revenues to the recipient (the Department of Public Health can approve as low as 5%), and joint ventures must return at least 25% of gross profits. The selected institute, "in consultation with the department," runs a licensing program to "maximize the revenue" and serves as "a clearinghouse and approval center" for every commercialization agreement under the measure.
The discount works in two stages. For the first 12 months of commercial sales, California patients, hospitals and insurers may not be charged more than the price anywhere else in the United States. After that, the first nine months of sales data set a "national average price, excluding California," and the California price must sit at least 20% below it, recalculated every year.
The LAO does not treat the royalty as a repayment plan. Revenue "is uncertain but could be significant," its analysis says, and "the timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state's bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades." Its ballot summary says the state "could recover part or all of this cost in subsequent decades." The reference point in California's own history is CIRM's first royalty check, $190,345.87, 14 years after Prop 71.
LAO fiscal estimate changed from $500 million a year for 25 years to $500 million to $600 million for about 20 years:
The LAO's ballot analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) estimates the General Fund cost of repaying the bond at "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years," about one-quarter of 1% of the state's General Fund budget, with the total cost "about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation)" than paying up front. Its December 17, 2025 letter to the Attorney General, written when the measure was still a petition, said "about $500 million each year over a 25-year period." That earlier figure is the one printed on the petition and in the ballot argument against the measure, which says taxpayers "would be committed to roughly $500 million in annual debt payments for the next 25 years." The two are different versions of the same estimate, not a disagreement.
The LAO also flags indirect effects it cannot size: new treatments could raise or lower costs for Medi-Cal, and the in-state purchasing rule could lift employment and taxable income. The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) puts the measure in context: the state is repaying about $80 billion of General Fund bonds, has about $40 billion more authorized but unsold, and pays about $6 billion a year in debt service, about 3% of General Fund revenue. Propositions 1 and 38 together would add about $1 billion a year, about half of 1%.
Proposition 38's Yes side reports $76.2 million from its top donors and its only opposition committee $3,782:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), updated October 14, shows $76.2 million in support of Prop 38 from two committees, the largest support figure for any measure on the ballot except Proposition 42. The main committee, "Yes on 38: Californians for Life-Saving Immunology Research and Cures, sponsored by the Michelson Center for Public Policy," lists four top contributors: Gary K. Michelson, $40 million; the Michelson Center for Public Policy's own Yes on 38 committee, $21.2 million, whose top contributor is Michelson; Meyer Luskin, $5 million; and the California Democratic Party, $15,595.20. The Center's committee lists one contributor, Michelson, at $10 million. Luskin is the institute's co-founder and treasurer.
The FPPC lists no opposing committee because none has reached the $1 million reporting threshold. The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-38-authorizes-bonds-immunology-research-initiative-statut), which counts all reported contributions through October 6, shows $64.2 million for the two Yes committees and $3,782 for the committee "No on Proposition 38." The petition that qualified the measure was paid for by "Californians for Immunology Research and Cures, sponsored by the Michelson Center for Public Policy," with major funding from Michelson, his affiliated entity and Luskin, according to the Secretary of State's Official Top Funders (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/top-funders/2006-top-funders-02-25-26.pdf) filing.
The arguments over Proposition 38 pit federal research cuts against ballot-box science:
The Yes argument (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Susan Disney Lord of Alzheimer's Los Angeles, Eugene P. Brandon of the ALS Association and Dr. Brian Shuch of the Kidney Cancer Association, says "massive federal funding cuts and uncertainty are disrupting vitally needed medical research" and that Prop 38 "creates a stable source of funding." It says the measure "is designed to pay for itself WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS," cites the 20% discount, the 2% administrative cap, the audits and the bar on for-profit grantees, and promises "tens of thousands of good-paying jobs." Quoted supporters include Stanford immunologist Mark Davis and cancer survivor Laurie Adami. The rebuttal to the No argument repeats that "YES ON 38 IS DESIGNED TO PAY FOR ITSELF."
The No argument, signed by Robert M. Kaplan of Stanford's Clinical Excellence Research Center, says the measure "continues the use of ballot initiatives to direct research funding toward selected topics" when California "has already created separate funding programs for stem cell research and precision medicine." It argues that borrowing "is an inappropriate way to finance scientific research," that "universities rarely commercialize new therapies on their own," and that the discount "could incentivize companies to prioritize selling these products in other states." It points to Senator Wiener's proposal for "a state-funded research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health," adding, "Although the legislation has not advanced, it received support from the University of California." Arguments were filed before the Legislature acted; the bill has since been signed and will appear on the March 2028 ballot. Kaplan's rebuttal calls the pay-for-itself claim "speculative."
Neither argument names the institute. The guide notes that ballot arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 38 leads 55% to 42% with Newsom and both parties in support and editorial boards opposed:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 55% yes, 42% no and 3% undecided. Democrats support it 76% to 21%, independents 54% to 43%, and Republicans oppose it 76% to 23%. Voters aged 18 to 34 back it 68% to 30% while those 55 and older split 50% to 47%. Renters support it 68% to 31% and homeowners 51% to 46%. Only 1% named it the measure they were most interested in. UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it.
Governor Newsom's campaign released (https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/gov-newsom-announces-position-statewide-185935591.html) his positions on October 9: yes on Prop 38, as on the ballot's two other bond measures, Propositions 1 and 37. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) both support it, which makes it one of two measures the parties agree on; the other is Prop 44, which both oppose. The Republican endorsement runs against the party's own voters in PPIC's poll. Xavier Becerra's July list (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/?p=551) of positions covers six measures and does not mention Prop 38.
The Voter Information Guide lists the Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Los Angeles, the Kidney Cancer Association and the American Nurses Association\California in support, and Kaplan alone against. The editorial boards we read all recommend a no vote: the Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317166634.html) and McClatchy's other California papers (September 30), the San Francisco Chronicle (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) (October 3), the Mercury News and East Bay Times (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/endorsement-no-on-california-proposition-38-an-8-4-billion-money-grab-immunotherapy-ucla-research-ballot-measure/) (October 13) and the Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-props-1-and-38-would-only-bring-more-debt-for-california/) (October 14). The No campaign lists (https://votenoonprop38.org/endorsements) six more boards, including the San Diego Union-Tribune and the Orange County Register, along with the League of Women Voters of California, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California

This institute could get $4 billion from a ballot measure. With just three workers, is it ready?
by
Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026

In summary
One research institute will receive $4.2 billion in bond money if voters approve Proposition 38 in November. Currently only one institute in the state meets the criteria to qualify for the money.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
The science research institute that would likely receive $4.2 billion in public taxpayer money if voters approve Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) this November had only three employees as of last month — far fewer than the 51 staffers it planned to have hired by last year.
Public statements and public records CalMatters (https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28824106-responsive-documents-26-7631-redacted-copy/?q=email&mode=document#document/p1)obtained raise questions about how well prepared the institute is to shepherd so much money if the bond measure passes.
Prop. 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion in bonds for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system, with an emphasis on finding treatments for Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The ballot language stipulates that a single, unnamed research institute would receive half the bond’s money to conduct research and partner with other researchers if it meets highly specific criteria. Bonds are a type of debt that must be repaid.
Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s principal funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign.
READ NEXT
This CA proposition will send $4 billion to a single nonprofit. Who’s behind it? (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/)
July 31, 2026 August 3, 2026
Backers of the proposition said state bond money is needed to stabilize research funding after President Donald Trump repeatedly attempted (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/) to cut existing and future federal science grants.
The measure’s critics say Prop. 38 is well-intentioned but poorly designed because it overlooks the many established public and nonprofit university and hospital research labs in California. They also say California should not subsidize subsets of scientific research and instead should support research more broadly.
CalMatters obtained documents that included the five-year business plan of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The plan was part of the formal affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute, which the two parties signed in August 2024. Among other details, the agreement requires the institute to pay UCLA 7.5% of the net revenue of any drugs and technologies developed by the institute’s staff. The institute is one of the founding tenants at a UCLA-owned research park in West Los Angeles, where the institute is leasing 235,000 square feet of research space, the institute says.
Far fewer employees than plan called for
Between summer 2024 and summer 2025, the institute committed to hiring “approximately” 51 employees, including six executives, five “world-class” scientists who can lead research labs, and 40 other employees, such as data scientists, lab technicians, biologists and administrative personnel. Between 2025 and 2027, the institute would hire roughly 90 more workers, including 10 research lab leaders, according to the agreement.
But John Mazziotta, a senior UCLA official who also serves as a board member (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors) of the immunology institute, last month said the institute has hired just three employees: a chief operating officer, a general counsel, and a scientific advisor, and “they’re well into the search” for a director. Mazziotta, the CEO of UCLA Health and vice chancellor for health sciences at UCLA, made his comments during the Sept. 16 UC Regents meeting.
The Yes on Prop. 38 campaign has repeatedly refused to comment on whether the bond was written specifically for the immunology institute. Claudia Briggs, a spokesperson for the campaign, told CalMatters in July that whichever nonprofit receives the $4.2 billion portion of the bond fund should be a sophisticated one that “is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
At a September press conference, a Yes on Prop. 38 spokesperson appeared to confirm CalMatters’ findings that only one institute currently qualifies to be the one to receive half the bond money. “It is very likely that CIII, which is a research institute affiliated with UCLA, will qualify for half of the funds under the current criteria,” said Robin Swanson. CIII is the initialism for the immunology institute.
According to the five-year plan, the institute was supposed to spend $25 million on personnel between 2024-25 and 2025-26 and $45 million total on operating expenses in that time, including maintenance, utilities and rent. It was also supposed to spend an additional $167 million in that time on capital expenses, such as construction and demolition. However, Mazziotta told UC regents that the institute had so far spent a total of $20 million on “operating expenses, hires” and other expenses.
The Yes on 38 campaign refused CalMatters’ request to interview Michelson for this story, as did Michelson himself in a separate email. A spokesperson for the institute, Becky Warren, sent a written statement that didn’t answer CalMatters’ questions about employing far fewer people than the five-year plan laid out. Instead, she highlighted the promise of the institute and a few of its milestones, including signing the affiliation agreement with UCLA and clearing a state environmental review of its forthcoming research facility.
The institute won’t get state bond money if it isn’t ready to begin work, “plain and simple,” wrote Swanson, the Yes on 38 spokesperson, in an email. She stressed that though the institute very likely qualifies, the ultimate decision (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/#:~:text=The%20bond%20measure%20language%20says%20that%20if%20no%20institute%20qualifies%2C%20the%20California%20Department%20of%20Public%20Health%20can%20adjust%20the%20criteria%20to%20select%20a%20winning%20institute.%C2%A0) to award half the bond funding is up to the California Department of Public Health.
Institute facility will be built by 2028
The UCLA research park that houses the institute isn’t slated to be fully built until at least late 2028, according to the agenda item (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/sept26/f3.pdf) of the September UC regents meeting. The research park is a former mall UCLA acquired in late 2023 that’s now undergoing major retrofitting.
But the 2024 affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute anticipated this. The agreement permitted the institute to use UCLA health research space on another campus property on an interim basis. Mazziotta told regents that research is underway there.

Mazziotta also told the regents the institute’s construction costs are not fully funded — it still needs roughly $100 million. He said UCLA was in serious talks with a donor to provide about $50 million to the institute.
If Prop. 38 passes, the bond funding would be provided in increments (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=shall%20not%20apply.-,130375.,-Solely%20for%20the) based on how often the institute requests new money that senior state officials approve. If all the funds are depleted, Californians would repay the bond (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm) at a rate of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years.
Institute would be exempt from public records act
CalMatters submitted the public records request to UCLA, which must comply with the California Public Records Act. The institute, as a private nonprofit, does not have to comply. And while Prop. 38 would channel billions of dollars in taxpayer money to the institute, the proposition’s language specifically exempts the nonprofit that will receive the $4.2 billion from state public meetings laws, political reform laws and the public records act. The other half of the funds would go to a council that’ll pick projects led by researchers from a limited pool of universities and nonprofits. The council would generally (https://yeson38.com/read-the-measure/#:~:text=The%20Political%20Reform%20Act%20of%201974%20(Title%209%20(commencing%20with%20Section%2081000)%20of%20the%20Government%20Code)%20shall%20apply%20to%20the%20council%2C%20except%20as%20provided%20in%20this%20section.) be governed by the state’s political reform act, which prohibits financial self-dealing.
Briggs defended the institute’s exemption in Prop. 38, writing that applying state transparency laws to existing private organizations would “not fit well with how private entities are organized and operate.” Instead, she noted the selected nonprofit institute would be required to publish annual reports on its research progress and financial plans plus commit to annual state audits, among other disclosures written into the ballot measure.
Still unclear to the UC regents is the relationship between UCLA and the institute on matters of public disclosure. Four senior UCLA officials sit on the institute’s board. So is a document held by those UCLA officials public because it’s related to UCLA affairs or private because it’s related to the institute’s affairs? UC’s general counsel couldn’t explain where that dividing line is after a regent member asked him. The regent member, Michael Cohen, said he wants more clarity when the regents meet again in November.
Gov. Gavin Newsom and the California Democratic Party endorsed (https://yeson38.com/newsroom/press-releases/) Prop. 38, as have dozens of patient and research advocacy groups, plus the state GOP. The evidence strongly leans "no." Key points:

Against (No):
1. Half the money ($4.2B) is effectively earmarked for a single unnamed institute (CIII at UCLA), whose co-founder/chair Gary Michelson wrote the measure and has given $40-61M+ to the campaign. Criteria tailor-made. This is a serious governance/corruption concern.
2. The institute is exempt from California Public Records Act, Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act, and Political Reform Act — despite receiving $4.2B of taxpayer money. Huge transparency problem.
3. Institute readiness: only 3 employees as of Sept 2026; facility not fully built until late 2028; construction not fully funded (needs ~$100M more).
4. Bonds are an inappropriate financing tool for research (operating expenses), costing ~10% more than paying up front. $500-600M/year for ~20 years (total ~$12B) from the General Fund, competing with schools, health care, housing.
5. The measure locks in a single narrow research field for decades and cannot be amended except by 2/3 Legislature, and never as to allocation/disbursement.
6. "Pays for itself" claim is speculative — LAO says revenue uncertain, could take decades; CIRM precedent: first royalty check $190K in 2018, 14 years after Prop 71.
7. A better alternative exists: SB 895, signed by Newsom Sept 30, 2026, places a $7.5B science and health research bond on the March 2028 ballot, creating a state foundation with open-meeting requirements, covering broader fields. So voters rejecting Prop 38 does not mean no research funding — a cleaner, broader, more accountable version is already scheduled.
8. Nearly every editorial board opposes (12 major boards), plus League of Women Voters, Common Cause, Consumer Watchdog, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The American Association of Immunologists' own policy committee recommended rescinding endorsement.
9. The grant half is also restrictive: council members select grants from among their own member organizations; members may vote on grants to entities in the same field as their employer and on diseases affecting themselves/family — conflict-of-interest carve-outs.

For (Yes):
- Federal research funding cuts under Trump create a real gap; immunology/immunotherapy is a promising field.
- Endorsed by Newsom, both state parties, many patient advocacy groups (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's LA, ALS Association, Kidney Cancer Association, ANA/CA), graduate student/postdoc union.
- 20% drug discount for Californians, 10% revenue to state, 2% admin cap, audits, no for-profit grantees, California supplier purchasing.
- Polls show 57% support.
- Cost is only ~0.25% of General Fund.

Weighing: The design flaws are serious — a $4.2B sole-source earmark to a private, non-transparent institute founded by the measure's own funder, financed with 20 years of general obligation debt, unamendable, when a cleaner and broader $7.5B research bond is already scheduled for March 2028 through the legislative process with open-meeting requirements. The near-unanimous opposition from editorial boards across the ideological spectrum, the League of Women Voters, Common Cause, and taxpayer groups, plus the internal revolt at the American Association of Immunologists, all point to "no."

Also note: the "no" vote doesn't kill immunology research funding — SB 895 offers a better path. That's a decisive factor.

- Endorsed by Newsom, both state parties, many patient advocacy groups (Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's LA, ALS Association, Kidney Cancer Association, ANA/CA), graduate student/postdoc union.

The evidence strongly leans "no." Key points:

Against (No):
1. Half the money ($4.2B) is effectively earmarked for a single unnamed institute (CIII at UCLA), whose co-founder/chair Gary Michelson wrote the measure and has given $40-61M+ to the campaign. Criteria tailor-made. This is a serious governance/corruption concern.

3. Institute readiness: only 3 employees as of Sept 2026; facility not fully built until late 2028; construction not fully funded (needs ~$100M more).
4. Bonds are an inappropriate financing tool for research (operating expenses), costing ~10% more than paying up front. $500-600M/year for ~20 years (total ~$12B) from the General Fund, competing with schools, health care, housing.
5. The measure locks in a single narrow research field for decades and cannot be amended except by 2/3 Legislature, and never as to allocation/disbursement.
6. "Pays for itself" claim is speculative — LAO says revenue uncertain, could take decades; CIRM precedent: first royalty check $190K in 2018, 14 years after Prop 71.
7. A better alternative exists: SB 895, signed by Newsom Sept 30, 2026, places a $7.5B science and health research bond on the March 2028 ballot, creating a state foundation with open-meeting requirements, covering broader fields. So voters rejecting Prop 38 does not mean no research funding — a cleaner, broader, more accountable version is already scheduled.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES on 38 supports life-saving immunology research to cure and prevent diseases like cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer’s. Strong accountability including independent audits. Mandates 20% Rx discount. Designed to ensure no cost to taxpayers. YES on 38 could save your life and someone you love. Alzheimer’s Association, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research urge YES on 38!
www.YESon38.com
CON
California should continue supporting biomedical research, but Proposition 38 is the wrong approach. It would commit taxpayers to decades of new bond debt while limiting California’s flexibility to address changing health priorities. Research funding should be guided through the normal budget process—not by ballot initiatives.

PROP
38
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR IMMUNOLOGY MEDICAL RESEARCH. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Medical Research and Development (R&D) Is a Multi- Stage Process. The first stage of this process is basic research, which focuses on discovering new knowledge about how the human body works. The next stage is applied and clinical research, which aims to develop and test treatments for specific diseases. Universities do most of the basic research, while companies do most of the applied and clinical research. The third R&D stage is to have regulators review new treatments to make sure they are safe and effective. If a new treatment is approved, then it may be used on patients. Most R&D projects do not make it through all of these stages.
Medical R&D Is Funded in Various Ways. Funding for medical R&D in the United States totaled about $300 billion in 2023. Companies and government agencies (such as the National Institutes of Health) are the major funding sources for R&D nationally and in California. Beyond these funding sources, California voters have approved two ballot measures- Proposition 71 (2004) and Proposition 14 (2020)- giving the state authority to issue general obligation bonds to fund specified medical research. Combined, the two measures allowed the state to issue $8.5 billion in bonds for stem cell research. Bonds are a way for the state to borrow money, then repay it with interest over time. A general obligation bond is typically repaid from the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) For more information about bonds, see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.
PROPOSAL
New Bond for Specified Medical Research. Proposition 38 allows the state to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond for research in immunology and immunotherapy. Immunology is the study of the body’s immune system and how it protects the body from abnormal cells and other causes of disease. Immunotherapy develops treatments that help the immune system fight diseases more effectively. The measure requires that at least $4.2 billion of the bond funds be used for immunology research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. No more than 2 percent of total bond funds may be used for state administrative costs. Payments on the bond would come from the state General Fund.
Supports a Research Institute. About half of the bond funds would go to a research institute specializing in immunology and immunotherapy. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would select the institute. The selected institute must meet several criteria, including criteria related to its size, funding, and collaboration with a University of California (UC) campus. The institute would use the bond funds for research. Each year, the institute must issue a public report on its activities and have an independent financial audit.
Supports Research Grants. A council would give out the other half of bond funds as competitive research grants focused on immunology and immunotherapy. The council would consist of representatives from 7 UC campuses and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions in California. The council would set research priorities and select grant recipients from among its member organizations. Similar to the institute, the council would have public reporting and audit requirements.
Requires 10 Percent of Revenue From Discoveries First Be Used to Repay the State. Proposition 38 requires that the institute, in consultation with CDPH, try to generate the most revenue possible from the funded research. (Research, for example, could lead to the development of a new medical treatment.) Ten percent of any revenue generated must be given to the state. This revenue must first go into the state General Fund until it repays the cost of the research bond (the amount borrowed plus the interest). Any additional revenue would be used for future immunology and immunotherapy research.
Has Two Other Notable Provisions.
Requires Purchases From California Suppliers. Grant recipients must buy at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers when reasonably possible.
Requires California Patient Discount. Any treatment developed through funded research and sold in California must generally be offered at a 20 percent discount.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost of $500 Million to $600 Million Annually for About 20 Years to Repay the Bond. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years . The annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 10 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up-front with money it already has.
Potential State Revenue From Research Discoveries. The state could receive revenue from research funded by Proposition 38. The amount of revenue is uncertain but could be significant. It would depend on how many research projects lead to marketable treatments and how much money any given treatment generates. The timing of these revenues and how long it would take to offset the state’s bond cost is also uncertain, but could take decades.
Potential Indirect Fiscal Effects. Proposition 38 likely would have some indirect fiscal effects, particularly on costs for state health programs (such as Medi-Cal, which pays for health care for low-income Californians). For example, if the funded research leads to new medical treatments, the average cost of patient care could either increase or decrease. As a result, the overall effect on program costs is uncertain.

## Half the money seems earmarked for a research center co-founded by Prop 38’s billionaire backer
SAN DIEGO — Internal emails obtained by STAT show that the American Association of Immunologists, the field’s leading scientific society, is sharply divided over California’s Proposition 38, even though it would provide $8.4 billion in taxpayer dollars for the type of research its members do.
The emails show that the association’s policy and advocacy committee met in July and later recommended that the organization rescind its endorsement of the measure after learning that Prop 38 would likely yield a windfall for a research center co-founded by the billionaire philanthropist who is its leading backer.
But the association’s council, its governing body, voted in August to maintain the endorsement after meeting with the philanthropist, Gary Michelson.
...
In one email, AAI’s director of government affairs, Jacob Schumacher, wrote that five members of the association’s council voted to keep the endorsement, with one opposed and two abstentions.

California’s Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research and send half to one UCLA-affiliated institute
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research. The measure's seven criteria for the institute that receives half the money match the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder has given the campaign at least $50 million. Here is the full picture.
by
Dr. Jennifer Trimpey | Specialist (https://californiatoday.com/author/jennifer-trimpey/)
Updated
October 16, 2026

Proposition 38 would let California borrow $8.4 billion to pay for research in immunology and immunotherapy, the science of using the body's immune system to prevent and treat disease. Half of the money would go to a single nonprofit research institute chosen by the state Department of Public Health under seven criteria written into the measure. The other half would be awarded as competitive grants by a council of university representatives. At least $2.1 billion of each half must be spent on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year from the General Fund for about 20 years.
Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," is an initiative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/) placed on the ballot by petition. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the most one-sided money race among them: $76.2 million in top-donor support against an opposition committee that has reported $3,782. It led 55% to 42% in PPIC's September survey, the only public poll to test it. Governor Gavin Newsom and both major parties support it; every newspaper editorial board we could read opposes it.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) This guide covers what the text does, the three research bonds California has already approved or scheduled, the organization the institute criteria describe, the measure's transparency rules, the royalty and discount provisions, the cost, the money behind each side, the arguments and the polling.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion and split it between one institute and a grant council:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) adds a new division to the Health and Safety Code authorizing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, the kind the state repays from the General Fund with interest. After bond costs and a cap of 2% for state administration, the proceeds are split two ways:
50% to "a single nonprofit medical research institute" selected by the Department of Public Health "for the purpose of conducting or directing health science research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy." The department must sign a funding agreement with the institute within 90 days of the measure taking effect and review it every five years. The measure also appropriates $100 million from the General Fund as a start-up loan to the institute, to be repaid from bond proceeds.
50% to competitive grants for public and nonprofit universities and nonprofit research institutions, awarded "as individualized grants for specific research projects through an application process," not as block grants. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council decides who gets them. Its seven-member executive committee is appointed by the chancellors of UC Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco, and that committee appoints 10 to 15 more members from other California nonprofit universities and research institutions, for a council of 17 to 22. UCLA's appointee serves as the council's first chair.
Each half carries a floor: "not less than" $2.1 billion must be spent on "the prevention, treatment, and cure of cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease." Grants are limited to researchers and projects "primarily located within this state," indirect costs are capped at 20% of a grant, and no money may go to for-profit companies. Every grant recipient must offer the selected institute "the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on the funded research," and must offer UCLA the same opportunity on any clinical trials.
Proposition 38's $8.4 billion is splitting evenly between one nonprofit research institute and a council-run grant program, with $2.1 billion of each half reserved for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. The measure can be amended only by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature, and never on "the allocation and disbursement of bond proceeds or the purposes for which bond proceeds may be expended."
California has borrowed for medical research twice before and has a third research bond scheduled for 2028:

California is the exception among states. Voters approved Proposition 71 in 2004, which authorized $3 billion in bonds for stem cell research and created the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, and Proposition 14 in 2020, which added $5.5 billion. Both were citizen initiatives. CIRM describes itself as a "taxpayer-funded agency" with a public governing board, and its revenue-sharing rules sent the state its first royalty check (https://blog.cirm.ca.gov/2018/02/12/california-gets-first-royalty-check-from-stem-cell-agency-investments/), for $190,345.87, in February 2018, 14 years after Prop 71 passed.
A third research bond is already on the calendar. Senate Bill 895, by Senator Scott Wiener, passed both houses on August 31 and was signed (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/30/at-the-top-of-the-golden-gate-bridge-governor-newsom-signs-his-final-bill-investing-in-californias-next-generation-of-innovation/) by Governor Newsom on September 30 as the last bill of the session. It places a $7.5 billion science and health research bond on the March 7, 2028 primary ballot and creates a California Foundation for Science and Health Research inside the Government Operations Agency to award grants, loans and contracts across "biomedical, behavioral health, and climate research" and other fields, with the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act applying to its council, according to the chaptered bill (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/sb895-ch1040.pdf). If Prop 38 passes, voters will have been asked to approve $15.9 billion of research bonds in 16 months.
